en: Points of Controversy The Great Fifty-Section Second Chapter
The Discourse on Gradual Realization:
Is there such a thing as gradual realization?
Yes, there is.
Does one develop the path of stream-entry gradually?
One should not say so.
Does one develop the path of stream-entry gradually? One should not say so.
“Yes,” [you say].
“Does one realize the fruit of stream-entry by way of gradual stages?
You should not say so.
Is it gradual realization?
Yes. Does one develop the path of the once-returner gradually? Yes.
It should not be said so.
[Is it then true that] one develops the path of the once-returner by way of successive stages? Yes.
Does one realize the fruit of once-returning by way of gradual realization?
One should not say so.
Is there gradual realization?
“Yes,” [you say].
“Does one develop the path of non-returning gradually?
One should not say so.
Does he, by gradual stages, develop the path of non-returning? Yes.
Does he, by gradual stages, realize the fruit of non-returning?
It should not be said so.
Is there a gradual realization? Yes.
"One develops the path to arahantship gradually"?
One should not say so.
"One develops the path to arahantship gradually"? One should not say so.
“Yes,” [you say].
“Does one realize the fruit of arhatship by way of successive stages?
One should not say so.
What does a person practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry abandon by the vision of suffering?
They abandon personality-belief, doubt, adherence to rules and observances, and the defilements associated with them—one quarter each.
One quarter is a stream-enterer, one quarter is not yet a stream-enterer, and one quarter has attained and acquired the fruit of stream-entry.
He has attained it, realized it, entered upon and dwells in it; he dwells having touched it with his body.
He dwells having touched it with his body for one-fourth [of the time]; for one-fourth [of the time] he does not dwell having touched it with his body.

At most seven times reborn, or passing from family to family, or a single-seeder, he is endowed with verified confidence in the Buddha, in the Dhamma …pe… in the Saṅgha …pe… and is endowed with the virtues dear to the Noble Ones.
"Is one not endowed with even a fourth part of the virtues dear to the Noble Ones?
One should not say so.
[This applies] by the vision of the origin... and so forth.
What does one abandon by the vision of cessation?
... [and] by the vision of the path?
One abandons the view of a personal body, doubt, adherence to rules and observances, and a quarter of the defilements associated with them.

A quarter is a stream-enterer; a quarter is not a stream-enterer. A quarter has attained, acquired, reached, realized, and entered upon the fruit of stream-entry, dwelling having touched it with the body;
a quarter does not dwell having touched it with the body. A quarter is one who will be reborn seven times at most, one who goes from family to family, or a single-seeder, [dedicated] to the Buddhas.

"Is one who possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha, [possesses unwavering confidence] in the Dhamma …pe… [possesses unwavering confidence] in the Saṅgha …pe… and possesses the virtues dear to the Noble Ones,
not possessed of a fourth part of the virtues dear to the Noble Ones?
One should not say so …pe….
What does a person practicing for the realization of the fruit of once-returning abandon through the vision of suffering?
They abandon coarse sensual lust, coarse ill will, and a quarter of the defilements associated with them.
A quarter is a once-returner, a quarter is not a once-returner, and a quarter has attained the fruit of once-returning.

"Has it been obtained, attained, realized, and entered upon so that one dwells having contacted it with the body? One dwells having contacted it with the body; one does not dwell having contacted even a fourth part with the body?
"One should certainly not say this... [and so forth].
What does one abandon through the vision of the origin?
... through the vision of cessation?
... through the vision of the path?
One abandons coarse sensual lust, coarse ill will, and the defilements associated with them—one quarter [of these].
One quarter is that of a once-returner; one quarter is not that of a once-returner. One quarter is the attainment, acquisition, realization, and reaching of the fruit of once-returning;
having entered upon it, one dwells there, touching it with the body. One quarter...
“Does he not dwell having touched it with the body?
One should not say so… [etc.
…What does a person practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning abandon by the vision of suffering?
He abandons the subtle residual lust for sensual pleasures, the subtle residual ill will, and the defilements associated with them—one quarter at a time.
One quarter he is a non-returner; one quarter he is not a non-returner;
one quarter he has attained, acquired, reached, realized, entered, and dwells in the fruit of non-returning, having touched it with his body. One quarter he is not...

Does one abide having touched [the goal] with the body: a quarter who attains final nibbāna in the interval … a quarter who attains final nibbāna upon landing … a quarter who attains final nibbāna without exertion … a quarter who attains final nibbāna with exertion … a quarter who is a non-returner bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm;
and a quarter who is neither a non-returner nor bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm?
It should not be said thus … [as before] … by the vision of the origin … [as before] … by the vision of cessation … [as before].
What does one abandon through the vision of the path?
One abandons the latent tendency of sensual lust, the latent tendency of ill will, and a fourth part of the associated defilements.
A fourth part is a non-returner, a fourth part is not a non-returner, and a fourth part has attained and realized the fruit of non-returning.
He has attained it, realized it, entered upon it and dwells in it; he dwells having touched it with his body, while one quarter he dwells without having touched it with his body:

[one who attains] parinirvāṇa in the interval … [one who attains] parinirvāṇa upon landing … [one who attains] parinirvāṇa without exertion … [one who attains] parinirvāṇa with exertion … [one who goes] upstream to the Akaniṣṭha realm—one quarter.
Is it not the case that one who is "bound upstream,
heading toward the Akaniṭṭha realm" cannot be so described?
… [as before] … What does a person practicing for the realization of Arahantship abandon by the vision of suffering?
He abandons a fourth part of attachment to the fine-material realm, attachment to the immaterial realm, conceit, restlessness, ignorance, and the defilements associated with them.
A fourth part he is an arahant; a fourth part he is not an arahant.
A fourth part he has attained, acquired, reached, realized, and entered upon, dwelling having touched it with the body; a fourth part he dwells having not touched with the body.
He dwells... with one-fourth [of his defilements] free from lust... free from hatred... free from delusion...

having done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, completely liberated through final knowledge, with the cross-bar removed, the moat filled in, the pillar uprooted, without bolts, noble, with banner lowered, with burden dropped, detached, a victor in battle who has won a well-fought victory—suffering [is ended].
For him, what was to be fully understood has been fully understood; origination has been abandoned; cessation has been realized; the path has been developed;

that which was to be directly known has been directly known; that which was to be fully understood has been fully understood; that which was to be abandoned has been abandoned; that which was to be developed has been developed...
[and so on] ...that which was to be realized has been realized. Is it not the case that the fourth part of what was to be realized has not yet been realized?
It should not be stated thus ... [as before] ...
What does one abandon through the vision of the origin, through the vision of cessation, and through the vision of the path?
One abandons attachment to form, attachment to the formless, conceit, restlessness, ignorance, and a fourth part of the defilements associated with them.

One quarter is an arahant; one quarter is not an arahant. One quarter has attained, acquired, reached, realized, and entered upon and dwells in the state of arahantship, having touched it with the body; one quarter does not dwell having touched it with the body.
One quarter is free from lust... free from hatred... free from delusion... one who has done what was to be done, laid down the burden... [and so forth].

Having attained his own goal, with the fetters of existence utterly destroyed, liberated through right knowledge, he has removed the crossbar, filled in the moat, pulled out the pillar, and is without bolts;
he is noble, with banner lowered, with burden laid down, detached, a victor who has won the victory.
Suffering has been fully understood by him, its origin abandoned, its cessation realized, and the path cultivated; that which was to be directly known has been directly known.
Is that which is to be fully understood fully understood; that which is to be abandoned abandoned;
that which is to be developed developed …pe… that which is to be realized realized, while a fourth part of what is to be realized has not been realized?
One should certainly not say so …pe….
Is a person practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry to be called one who is "practicing" while perceiving suffering?
Yes. Is he to be called one who is "established in the fruit" once suffering has been seen?
It should not be said so.
Should it be said that one who sees the origin [of suffering]... pe ...one who sees the cessation [of suffering] is a practitioner?
“Yes,” you say.
“Then one who has seen cessation should be said to be established in the fruit?
You must not say so.

Is a person practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry to be called "one practicing" while seeing the path, and to be called "one established in the fruit" when the path has been seen?
Yes.
Is one seeing suffering to be called "one practicing," and to be called "one established in the fruit" when suffering has been seen?
It should not be said thus … [as before] … Should it be said that one who sees the Path is called a "practitioner," and one for whom the Path has been seen is called "established in the fruit"?
Yes, it should.
"One who sees the origin [of suffering]... pe...
one who sees the cessation [of suffering] should be called a practitioner; one who has seen cessation should be called one established in the fruit.
Is this not so? It should not be said so... pe... [end of formula].
Is a person practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry to be called "one practicing while seeing suffering," and when suffering has been seen,
not to be called "one established in the fruit"? Yes.

One who is seeing the path should be called "one practicing" (paṭipannaka); when the path has been seen, should it not be said that "he should be called one established in the fruit"? It should not be so stated... [and so on].
One who perceives the origin [of suffering]...
one who perceives the cessation [of suffering] should be called "one practicing the way. When cessation has been seen, should it not be said that "one should be called 'established in the fruit'"?
“Yes.
[The opponent asks: “When one sees the path, should one be called ‘one who has entered upon the practice’? When the path has been seen, should it not be said that one is ‘established in the fruit’?”

It should not be said thus… [as before]… Is a person practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry to be called one who is "practicing" while perceiving suffering, but once suffering has been seen, no longer to be called so,
but rather to be called "established in the fruit"?
“Yes.
“Then is the vision of suffering useless?
“One should not say so. … [as before] …
One who sees the origin [of suffering]...
[and so on] ...one who sees cessation may be called "one practicing the way. When cessation has been seen, should it not be said that "he is established in the fruit"?
“Yes,” [you say].
“Then is the vision of cessation purposeless?
You should not say so … [as before] … .
If suffering is seen, are the four truths seen?
Yes. Is the truth of suffering the four truths? No.
It should not be said thus… [as before]… When the aggregate of form is seen as impermanent, are the five aggregates seen as impermanent?
Yes.
Is the aggregate of form the five aggregates?
One should not say so... [and so on] ...
When the eye-base is seen as impermanent, are the twelve bases seen as impermanent?
“Yes,” you say.
“Is the eye-base one of the twelve bases?
You should not say so… [and so on].
When the eye-element is seen as impermanent, are the eighteen elements seen as impermanent?
Yes. Are the eye-element and the eighteen elements [identical]? No.
It should not be said so … [as before] … When the eye-faculty is seen as impermanent, are the twenty-two faculties seen as impermanent?
Yes.
Is the eye-faculty one of the twenty-two faculties?
One should not say so... [and so on] ...
Does one realize the fruit of stream-entry by means of four knowledges?
“Yes,” [you say].
“Are there four fruits of stream-entry?
You should not say so …pe…
"One realizes the fruit of stream-entry by means of eight knowledges"?
Yes. "Are there eight fruits of stream-entry"? [No.]
It should not be said thus … [as before] … Does one realize the fruit of stream-entry by means of twelve knowledges? Yes.
"Are there twelve fruits of stream-entry?
"One should not say so. ...pe...
"Does one realize the fruit of stream-entry by means of forty-four knowledges?"
“Yes,” you say.
“Are there forty-four fruits of stream-entry?
You should not speak thus … [and so on] …
Is it the case that one realizes the fruit of stream-entry by means of seventy-seven knowledges?
Yes. Are there, then, seventy-seven fruits of stream-entry?
It should not be said thus … [as before] … Should it not be said that there is a gradual realization?
“Yes, [it is so].
“But was it not said by the Blessed One:
‘Bhikkhus, just as the great ocean slopes gradually, inclines gradually, and shelves gradually, not falling off abruptly;’”
“In the same way, monks, in this Dhamma and Vinaya there is gradual training, gradual performance, and gradual practice; there is no penetration of final knowledge all at once.
Is this indeed a sutta?
Yes, it is.
In that case, there is gradual realization.
Should it not be said that there is "gradual realization"?
“Yes.
[The opponent asks: “Has it not been said by the Blessed One:
‘Gradually, step by step, the wise one, ...’?”
Little by little, moment by moment,
like a smith purifying silver,
one should blow away one's own impurities.
Is it indeed a sutta? Yes.
Therefore, there is a gradual realization.
Is it the case that there is gradual realization? Yes.
Did not the Venerable Gavampati Thera say this to the bhikkhus: [and so forth]?
“Friends, I have heard this directly from the Blessed One, I have received it directly from him:
‘Bhikkhus, whoever sees suffering also sees the origin of suffering, also sees the cessation of suffering, and also sees the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
Whoever sees the origin of suffering also sees suffering, also sees the cessation of suffering, and also sees the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.’”
“He who sees the cessation of suffering also sees suffering, he also sees the origin of suffering, and he also sees the practice leading to the cessation of suffering;
he who sees the practice leading to the cessation of suffering also sees suffering, he also sees the origin of suffering, and he also sees the cessation of suffering.
Is this indeed a sutta?
“Yes, [it is so].
Therefore, it should not be said that “there is a gradual realization.”
Is there gradual realization? Yes.
But was it not said by the Blessed One:
“For one who has achieved the perfection of vision,
these three things are abandoned:
personality-belief, doubt, and
Whatever rules and observances there may be,
he is completely freed from the four states of misery and incapable of committing the six acts of immediate retribution.
Is it indeed a sutta? Yes.
Therefore, it should not be said—
“Gradual realization.
Is it gradual realization? Yes.
Has it not been said by the Blessed One:
“Bhikkhus, at whatever time the dustless, stainless Dhamma-eye arises in a noble disciple—
‘Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease’— with the arising of that vision, bhikkhus, three fetters are abandoned in the noble disciple:”
“Personality-belief, doubt, and adherence to rules and observances.
Is this indeed a sutta?
Yes, it is.
Therefore, it should not be said that there is a gradual realization.
The discussion on gradual realization is finished.
